title: Spectral and thermodynamic properties of supersymmetric quantum systems with self-adjoint deformed momentum
authors: J. A. Oke, F. A. Dossa
abstract: We establish a rigorous framework for quantum systems with geometric deformations by constructing a strictly self-adjoint deformed momentum operator through the generalized extended momentum operator (GEMO) formalism. Unlike previous approaches relying on boundary-condition hermiticity, our method ensures intrinsic self-adjointness for both linear ($μ(x)=αx$) and quadratic ($μ(x)=αx^{2}$) deformations within a unified non-Hermitian supersymmetric factorization scheme. This yields exact analytical spectra while revealing hidden $\mathfrak{su}(1,1)$ symmetry structures. Crucially, we provide the first complete thermodynamic characterization of such systems by analytically evaluating the partition function via the Euler--Maclaurin approximation. Geometric deformation fundamentally reshapes the density of states $ρ(E)$, producing distinct thermal signatures: a divergent heat capacity peak for linear deformation due to state accumulation near a maximal energy, and a saturation $C/k_{\mathrm{B}}\to 0.6$ (below the Dulong--Petit limit) for quadratic deformation. These results establish geometric deformation as a tunable parameter for engineering quantum thermodynamic responses in curved nanostructures.
summary: The paper develops a rigorous method using the Generalized Extended Momentum Operator (GEMO) formalism to study quantum systems under geometric deformations. It analytically solves the energy spectrum and provides the first complete thermodynamic characterization by calculating the partition function. The key finding is that the type of deformation dictates unique thermal responses, allowing for the engineering of quantum heat capacity in nanostructures.
main_problem: To establish a rigorous framework for quantum systems with geometric deformations by constructing a strictly self-adjoint deformed momentum operator.
main_result: The study predicts distinct thermal signatures: linear deformation causes a divergent heat capacity peak, while quadratic deformation leads to a saturation of $C/k_B 	o 0.6$ below the Dulong–Petit limit.
method: The authors use the Generalized Extended Momentum Operator (GEMO) formalism combined with an extended Supersymmetric Quantum Mechanics (SUSYQM) factorization scheme for spectral analysis, and employ the Euler–Maclaurin approximation for thermodynamic characterization.
model_or_system: The system is a one-dimensional quantum oscillator subjected to geometric deformations modeled by $\mu(x)$, analyzed in linear ($\mu(x)=\alpha x$) and quadratic ($\mu(x)=\alpha x^2$) cases. The Hamiltonian is derived from substituting the GEMO operator into the standard form.
key_observables: Energy spectra ($E_n$), Density of states ($ho(E)$), Internal energy ($U$), Entropy ($S$), and Heat Capacity ($C$).
important_parameters: Deformation parameter $\alpha$, Temperature ($ eta$ or $1/T$), and the effective curvature induced by $\mu(x)$.
main_assumptions: The method assumes geometric deformation can be modeled by $\mu(x)$ (linear or quadratic), and it relies on the Euler–Maclaurin approximation for calculating the partition function.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the evolution of energy levels ($E_n$) versus the deformation parameter $\alpha$ for both linear and quadratic cases, alongside plots showing thermodynamic quantities like heat capacity vs. inverse temperature ($ eta$).
paper_structure: The paper first develops the self-adjoint framework using GEMO/SUSYQM to find exact spectra for deformed Hamiltonians. It then calculates the partition function $Z( eta)$ and derives all key thermodynamic observables, comparing the distinct thermal responses of linear versus quadratic deformations.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful theoretical tool linking geometric structure (via momentum deformation) directly to measurable macroscopic quantum thermodynamic properties, which is highly relevant for designing novel quantum materials.

This increase becomes more pronounced as the deformation parameter 𝛼increases, reflecting an increase in the number of accessible energy states at high temperatures. Simultaneously, the free energy (𝐹) decreases with increasing temper- ature, which is characteristic of a thermally excited system. The effect of the deformation is manifested by a change in the slope of this decrease, highlighting the influence of 𝛼on the thermodynamic potential of the system.
